opus-5.5.text:
Thanks for having me. The main thing we wanted was to show how far you could get with a really simple setup. A lot of SWE-bench submissions at the time had elaborate scaffolding: multi-stage pipelines, hand-built workflows where step one is localize the file, step two is write a patch, step three is run tests. Those can work, but they're built around the limitations of the model.

Our view was that as the models get better, you want to get out of their way. So the reference agent is pretty minimal. It's basically a prompt, a bash tool, and a file editing tool, and then you let the model decide what to do and keep going until it thinks it's done. There's no fixed sequence of steps. The model explores the repo, reproduces the bug, makes the fix, and checks its own work, all in a loop it controls.

Part of the goal was to measure the model itself rather than the scaffolding. If you build a really clever harness, it's hard to tell how much of the score comes from the model and how much from the engineering around it. Keeping the agent simple gives a cleaner signal.

The other part was to give developers something they could actually learn from. We wanted people to look at it and think, "Oh, I can build this." A lot of what we learned was that the effort goes into the tools rather than the overall architecture. Making the tool descriptions really clear, designing the interfaces so the model is less likely to make mistakes, and thinking about it the way you'd write documentation for a junior engineer. That turned out to matter much more than any fancy orchestration.

r001.rationale: The response says developers should be able to learn from the agent and think, “I can build this,” but does not state that Anthropic wanted to share its implementation as a foundation for agents on Anthropic’s system.

fable-5.1.text:
Honestly, the biggest thing we wanted to show was that you don't need a lot of scaffolding to get a really strong result on SWE-bench. When we started looking at the leaderboard, a lot of the top entries had these very elaborate pipelines: specialized retrieval stages, hand-tuned prompts for each phase of the problem, ensembles that generate a bunch of candidate patches and then vote or run a separate model to pick the best one. All of that is clever, but it also means the human is doing a lot of the problem-solving ahead of time and baking it into the system.

What we wanted to do instead was get out of the model's way. Give it a bash tool, give it a file editing tool, write a reasonably clear system prompt, and then let it decide how to explore the repo, where to look, when to run tests, when it's done. The reference agent is really minimal. The whole thing fits in a few hundred lines, and most of the intelligence is in the model rather than in the harness.

Part of the motivation was measurement. If you wrap the model in heavy scaffolding, you're measuring the scaffold as much as the model, and it becomes hard to tell when the model actually got better at software engineering. A simple agent gives you a much cleaner signal. When we went from 3.5 Sonnet to the upgraded version, we didn't change the agent at all and the score jumped a lot, and that told us something real about the model.

The other motivation was that we think this is where the field is going anyway. As models get more capable, the right move is to trust them with more of the loop instead of less. A lot of the tricks people built in 2023 were compensating for weaknesses that are going away. So we wanted to publish something that people could actually use as a starting point, that reflected how we think agents should be built, rather than something optimized to squeeze out a few extra points on one benchmark.

r001.rationale: The response says Anthropic wanted to publish a usable starting point, but it does not state that the implementation was shared for building agents on Anthropic’s system.

astra-6.text: We wanted to build a really simple agent that would show what the model itself could do. With SWE-bench, you give it a GitHub issue and a repository, and it has to figure out what’s wrong and make the code changes to fix it. The idea was to give the model the tools it needed to explore the repo, edit files, and run tests, without putting a lot of specialized logic into the scaffolding. That way, it could serve as a useful starting point for people building their own agents.

r001.rationale: The response says the agent could be a starting point for people building their own agents, but does not clearly state that Anthropic intended to share its implementation for building agents on Anthropic’s system.

sol-6.1.text: We wanted to build the simplest possible agent that would let us measure the model’s ability to solve real software engineering problems. The goal wasn’t to get the highest SWE-bench score with a lot of custom scaffolding. It was to give the model straightforward tools to inspect the repository, edit files, and run tests, then see how far it could get. That gives us a useful baseline and makes it easier to understand improvements in the model itself.

r001.rationale: The response describes building a simple agent as a measurement baseline, but does not say Anthropic intended to share its implementation for others to build agents on its system.
